Get started with naxps

Source: vignettes/naxp.Rmd
naxp.Rmd
library(naxp)

A naxp maps text-based codes, e.g. postcodes, to integers and back again.

If you haven’t already, please first take the naxp quick tour.

Create a naxp

For the purpose of illustration, we’ll roll our own Netherlands postcode naxp1.

A Netherlands postcode is four digits followed by two letters, officially with a space between the digits and the two letters, although this is often omitted in electronic data.

This naxp accepts both forms (but treats the version with a space as the canonical version):

NL_postcode_x <- naxp_parse(r"(\9\9\9\9 \s!! \A\A)")
NL_postcode_x
#> <naxp> \9\9\9\9 \s!! \A\A
#> Maximum encoded value: 6760000

We’ve used a raw string, r"(...)", because naxps use backslashes (like regexes) and in a normal string every backslash would have to be doubled.

The !! syntax means

  • the preceding item makes no difference to the encoding whether or not it’s present, and
  • include it when decoding the encoded value back to text.

This naxp maps every postcode that fits the pattern to an integer from 1 to 6 760 000, with no gaps.

Let’s take it for a test drive:

postcodes_as_text <- c("1012 AB", "1012AB", "1012-AB", "not a postcode")
postcodes <- naxp_encode(postcodes_as_text, NL_postcode_x)
postcodes
#> <naxp_encoded[4]> \9\9\9\9 \s!! \A\A
#> [1] 1012 AB       1012 AB       <invalid (0)> <invalid (0)>
as.integer(postcodes)
#> [1] 684114 684114      0      0

Note that both 1012 AB and 1012AB were mapped to the same encoded value.

The invalid text, including 1012-AB, was mapped to 02.

We can go in the other direction, i.e. decode the encoded value back to text:

naxp_decode(postcodes) # No need for the naxp (NL_postcode_x)
#> [1] "1012 AB" "1012 AB" NA        NA
naxp_decode(684114L, NL_postcode_x) # Decoding raw numbers requires a naxp
#> [1] "1012 AB"
naxp_decode(0L, NL_postcode_x) # 0 means invalid -- it decodes to NA
#> [1] NA

As promised, decoding gives the form with the space, i.e. 1012 AB.

Note that the first line above did not need the original naxp because it is already included in the vector’s attributes.

Encoded values that are negative or greater than the maximum raise an error:

naxp_decode(6760001L, NL_postcode_x)
#> Error in `naxp_decode()`:
#> ! x[1] is 6760001, above the naxp's maximum encoded value of 6760000.

For convenience, you can check whether text is valid for a naxp and convert it to the canonical form without encoding it using the following functions:

naxp_accepts(postcodes_as_text, NL_postcode_x)
#> [1]  TRUE  TRUE FALSE FALSE
naxp_canonical_form(postcodes_as_text, NL_postcode_x)
#> [1] "1012 AB" "1012 AB" NA        NA

You can obtain properties of a naxp:

writeLines(naxp_pattern(NL_postcode_x)) # Text pattern used to define the naxp
#> \9\9\9\9 \s!! \A\A
naxp_max_encoded_value(NL_postcode_x) # Maximum encoded value
#> [1] 6760000
naxp_max_length(NL_postcode_x) # Maximum decoded text length
#> [1] 7

Encoded values in data

The naxp_encode() function returns a naxp_encoded vector of encoded values, an S3 class. As noted above, a naxp_encoded also includes the naxp used to encode the values.

A naxp_encoded looks like text when printed, including when it’s part of a data frame:

offices <- data.frame(
  office = c("Amsterdam", "Maastricht", "Head office"),
  postcode = naxp_encode(c("1012 AB", "6211 CA", "1012AB"), NL_postcode_x)
)
offices
#>        office postcode
#> 1   Amsterdam  1012 AB
#> 2  Maastricht  6211 CA
#> 3 Head office  1012 AB
offices[offices$postcode == "1012 AB", ]
#>        office postcode
#> 1   Amsterdam  1012 AB
#> 3 Head office  1012 AB

Comparing a naxp_encoded with text encodes the text before the comparison. This is why, in the above, the encoded values for "1012AB" and "1012 AB" both match "1012 AB".

sort() sorts by encoded value.

To turn bare encoded values, e.g. values read back from a database or a file, back into a naxp_encoded vector, use naxp_encoded():

naxp_encoded(c(684114, 0), NL_postcode_x)
#> <naxp_encoded[2]> \9\9\9\9 \s!! \A\A
#> [1] 1012 AB       <invalid (0)>

It checks every value, so an illegal one is an error:

naxp_encoded(6760001L, NL_postcode_x)
#> Error in `naxp_encoded()`:
#> ! values[1] is 6760001, above the naxp's maximum encoded value of 6760000.

naxp constraints in R

The naxp specification permits up to 264−1 encoded values but R does not have built-in 64-bit integers. Consequently,

  • naxps with a maximum encoded value up to 231−1 are stored as integer,
  • naxps with a maximum encoded value up to 253 are stored as double, otherwise
  • the functions that return or accept encoded values, such as naxp_encode() and naxp_decode(), raise an error3.

Standard naxps

Standard naxps are provided for widely used code systems. The benefits are:

  • Safety – a hand-written pattern can contain mistakes that silently change the encoding, whereas a standard one has been tested and is fixed for all time.
  • Consistent encoding – all variants of a standard encode consistently, i.e. any text accepted by two variants results in the same encoded value.
  • Commonality – the standards are the same in all languages in which naxps are implemented.
naxp_standards()[, c("id", "variant")]
#>                   id           variant
#> 1        uk-postcode           default
#> 2        uk-postcode  padding-tolerant
#> 3        uk-postcode padding-canonical
#> 4            eircode           default
#> 5            eircode      no-separator
#> 6        nl-postcode           default
#> 7        nl-postcode      no-separator
#> 8        nl-postcode   hyphen-tolerant
#> 9  flight-designator           default
#> 10 flight-designator            strict

We could have created our Netherlands postcode naxp using

NL_postcode_x2 <- naxp_standard("nl-postcode")
naxp_compare(NL_postcode_x, NL_postcode_x2)
#>   accepted_text        encoding canonical_forms 
#>         "equal"         "equal"         "equal"

All three relationships are “equal”, which means that our naxp and the standard one behave identically.

For detailed information on all available standard naxps, see naxp.org/standard.

Comparing and migrating naxps

In the above, we used naxp_compare() to check that our hand-written Netherlands postcode naxp was the same as the standard one. The definitions were the same so this was trivially true, but things are not always so simple.

Let’s imagine that we have new incoming postcode data that uses hyphen separators, e.g. 1012-AB (which is not uncommon in the Netherlands).

The naxp package provides a hyphen-tolerant variant for Netherlands postcodes, but is this safe to use without re-encoding the encoded values we’ve already stored?

Let’s find out:

NL_postcode_HT_x <- naxp_standard("nl-postcode", "hyphen-tolerant")
naxp_compare(NL_postcode_x, NL_postcode_HT_x)
#>   accepted_text        encoding canonical_forms 
#>     "subset_of"     "subset_of"         "equal"

This comparison tells us:

  • accepted_text being "subset_of" means the hyphen-tolerant naxp accepts all text the existing one does, and more.
  • encoding being "subset_of" means every text accepted by the existing naxp has the same encoded value under the hyphen-tolerant naxp, but the hyphen-tolerant naxp also accepts text that is invalid under the existing naxp.
  • canonical_forms being "equal" means both naxps decode to the same texts.

This means it is safe to replace the existing naxp with the hyphen-tolerant naxp. Here is the difference in practice:

postcodes_as_text
#> [1] "1012 AB"        "1012AB"         "1012-AB"        "not a postcode"

# Rejects "1012-AB":
as.integer(naxp_encode(postcodes_as_text, NL_postcode_x))
#> [1] 684114 684114      0      0

# Accepts "1012-AB":
as.integer(naxp_encode(postcodes_as_text, NL_postcode_HT_x))
#> [1] 684114 684114 684114      0

See naxp.org/migrate to play with an interactive version (which also helps interpret the results if you are considering migrating a naxp).

Errors

An invalid naxp pattern raises a naxp_error, which includes diagnostics about the error and its location.

naxp_parse(r"(\9\9\9\9 [A-)")
#> Error in `naxp_parse()`:
#> ! NAXP1025 at 9..10: This character set is not closed. Add a ']'.
#>   The error is at "[", after "\9\9\9\9 ".
#> See https://naxp.org/error-codes/#naxp1025

Use tryCatch() to obtain more information:

error <- tryCatch(naxp_parse(r"(\9\9\9\9 [A-)"), naxp_error = identity)
error$code
#> [1] "NAXP1025"
error$offset
#> [1] 9

The NAXP... error codes are the same in every naxp library.

Code generation

naxp_emit() allows you to generate source code in other languages, including C++, C# and JavaScript.

Go to naxp.org/code-gen to see this working in practice.
